solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Dick garnish? Cyclops had one

definitions.note: the definition is a surname standing for the first name that goes with it

parts.note: cress is a salad leaf used to garnish food
the one-eyed giant saying it himself: I'd a, that is I had a (one)

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about what to put on a dish, with the setter claiming to have had one himself.
explanation.walkthrough: Cressida Dick was Commissioner of London's Metropolitan Police; the Private Eye setter Cyclops speaks as the one-eyed giant, so 'Cyclops had one' becomes I'D A.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Cressida Dick headed the London police force, so her surname in the clue points to her first name.

clue.text: Bit of a joke model pursuing Robin

definitions.text: Bit of a joke model pursuing Robin

parts.note: surface reading: a fragment of a comedy figure, perhaps a model chasing a bird
setter's reading: the first word of a much-mocked three-wheeled car's full name, which goes along with Robin

explanation.walkthrough: The Reliant Robin was a British three-wheeled car, a standing joke for its habit of tipping over; the answer is one half of that model's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The maker's name is literally one bit of the car's name, and the car itself was widely treated as a laughing stock.

clue.text: Planned on making street lowlife, say, in charge

parts.note: ST is the standard abbreviation for street
a rat is a despicable person
e.g., for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say'
IC is the usual abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: Someone intended to turn a road into a haunt of low-lifes, with an example in command.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is four short abbreviations and synonyms laid end to end in the order they appear.
explanation.definitionFit: A strategic move is one carried out according to a deliberate scheme, so the adjective matches something done by design.

clue.text: Suffer: "No space for hot dog!"

parts.note: hot and in both mean fashionable
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A complaint that there's nowhere to put a frankfurter in a bun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot dog' reads as the sausage, but it splits into two words, and 'No space' tells you to write their synonyms closed up as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To incur a loss or penalty is to bring it upon yourself and so undergo it.

clue.text: Sailors ain't about to refrain from sex?

definitions.note: the question mark marks sex as one example of what is given up

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is a sailor; plural ABS

indicators.note: about can mean around or turned round, so these letters are moved into a different order

parts.note: the letters of the contraction, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A tongue-in-cheek doubt that seamen are about to give up sex.
explanation.walkthrough: AB (able-bodied seaman) is the crossword sailor. The apostrophe in ain't is ignored, leaving four letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to hold back from something voluntarily, and celibacy is a classic case of holding back.

clue.text: President almost gets disheartened Trumpists personal clean-up aids

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut off

parts.note: Joe Biden, US president

indicators.note: to lose the heart is to lose the middle, so only the outside letters stay

parts.note: first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A political sketch: the president nearly wins over dispirited Trump supporters, with a smutty twist.
explanation.walkthrough: President here is Biden, who with his last letter gone gives BIDE; 'disheartened' strips a word to its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A bidet is a low basin used for washing the private parts, a bathroom fixture for personal hygiene.

clue.text: Minister, who (had Sunak been one) would not be back in government?

parts.words: Minister, who (had Sunak been one) would not be back in government?
parts.note: surface reading: a cabinet minister whose return depended on the prime minister
setter's reading: split the surname as a comparative adjective plus a noun, the kind of person Sunak failed to be

explanation.surface: A dig at a prime minister who reappointed a controversial minister for lack of nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: Suella Braverman resigned as Home Secretary and was reappointed days later by Rishi Sunak; had he been more courageous, the clue says, he would not have brought her back.
explanation.definitionFit: Suella Braverman served as Home Secretary, a senior cabinet post in the British government.

clue.text: US city scam

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a Kansas cattle town of Wild West fame
second meaning: a crafty trick or swindle

explanation.walkthrough: Dodge City in Kansas is usually named in full, so the short form is a little loose.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a Kansas frontier town and is also informal for a cunning trick used to cheat or evade.

clue.text: Nasty wind brought about by rent trouble

parts.note: rent is the past participle of rend, meaning ripped
ado is fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: Flatulence caused by the stress of a landlord dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' reads as money for housing, but it is the verb form meaning torn.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a violent, destructive rotating storm, about as unpleasant as moving air can be.

clue.text: Minister has two Conservative leaders trapping Right in pathetic lie

indicators.note: to trap something is to hold it inside, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: C, the initial of Conservative, twice

indicators.note: something pathetic is feeble and in a sorry state, so these letters are knocked out of shape

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cabinet minister caught with two party leaders in a feeble right-wing lie.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes into LIE and the four letters are rearranged; the two C's then sit at either end. Minister switches from politics to the church.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister of religion is a member of the clergy, and a cleric is exactly that.

clue.text: Norm's defiant position on publicity about Republican

parts.note: to take a stand is to hold a defiant position

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: an ad is an advertisement
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: Someone called Norm takes a stubborn line on a political campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Norm's' looks like a man's name with a possessive; it is the definition followed by 'is'. 'On' just puts the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is an accepted level or rule that things are measured against, which is what a norm is.

clue.text: Satisfy yourself the state's utter crap, stifling British-American overtures

parts.note: MA is the postal abbreviation for Massachusetts, plus the possessive S

indicators.note: to stifle is to smother, so one piece closes round the other
crap describes something shoddy and messed up, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: an overture is an opening, so each word gives only its first letter

parts.note: the two initial letters

explanation.surface: A crude complaint that the country's in a dreadful state, with talk of a transatlantic deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utter' looks like an adjective intensifying the next word; it is the fodder, and 'crap' is the signal. MA is Massachusetts in US postal code.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving oneself sexual pleasure without a partner is the plain meaning of the word, put as a euphemism.

clue.text: see 22ac.
Mark — bastard's turned over the old lady

indicators.note: something turned over faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a git is a contemptible person, plus the possessive S
the old lady is slang for mother, MA

explanation.surface: Someone called Mark is accused of mugging an elderly woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Git is British slang for an unpleasant person. 'Mark' looks like a man's name addressed in the surface; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma is a mark of disgrace, and the word originally meant a brand or visible mark on the skin.

clue.text: High octane lad, not to be relied on

indicators.note: someone high is intoxicated and all over the place, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lad fuelled up on something potent is not dependable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High octane' reads as a phrase about fuel, but 'High' works alone as the signal and 'octane lad' is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Anecdotal evidence rests on personal stories rather than systematic study, so it cannot be trusted as proof.

clue.text: Pardon me — about to do a Jeffrey Archer?

indicators.note: about can mean turned round or reworked, so these letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An apology from someone about to behave like a notorious novelist and peer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pardon me' reads as an apology but supplies the letters. Jeffrey Archer is a British bestselling novelist and Tory peer, mocked by Private Eye for boasting of famous friends.
explanation.definitionFit: Name-dropping means casually mentioning famous acquaintances to impress, a habit the question mark pins on one well-known boaster.

clue.text: Fire former royal son and demand payment!

parts.note: Diana, Princess of Wales, known as Di
S is the abbreviation for son
to charge is to ask for money

explanation.surface: A call to sack a former royal's son and send him the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' reads as dismiss in the surface, which is also a valid sense of the answer; it equally fits firing a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: To discharge is both to let off a weapon and to dismiss an employee, so it matches either sense of the verb.

clue.text: Eric came over dessert

indicators.note: over can mean knocked over or reworked, so these letters are moved around

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of a man reaching a climax on a pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Came over' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'over' is the signal and 'Eric came' supplies the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice cream is a frozen sweet served at the end of a meal, a standard pudding.

clue.text: Strip, sticking one ball in box

indicators.note: sticking something in a place puts it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a carton is a cardboard box
O is round like a ball

explanation.surface: A striptease that involves putting a testicle in a container.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strip' reads as undress, but it is the noun, as in comic strip.
explanation.definitionFit: A comic strip is a sequence of drawn panels, and a cartoon is the same kind of drawing.

clue.text: Spar perhaps with Digger, then a Labour leader

parts.note: a miner digs for coal or ore
taken as written

indicators.note: a leader goes first, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: A boxing sparring session with a pit worker and then a Labour Party leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spar' reads as practise boxing, but it is a noun: a crystalline stone. 'Digger' also suggests an Australian, a common crossword sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Spar is a name for various crystalline minerals such as feldspar, so it is an example of the category.

clue.text: In earnest? Let's cosy up

indicators.note: in means inside, so the letters sit within the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A serious suggestion that the two of you get snug together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In earnest' reads as a set phrase meaning seriously; 'In' works alone as the signal, and the answer runs across the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: To nestle is to settle snugly against someone, which is what cosying up means.

clue.text: Couch potatoes right to be put in sale of rubbish?

indicators.note: putting something in places it inside, so one piece goes within the other
rubbish describes something worthless and broken, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Idle TV watchers who ought to be sold off in a junk sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sale of rubbish' reads as a jumble sale; 'rubbish' is actually the signal working on 'sale of'.
explanation.definitionFit: A loafer is an idler who lazes about, just like someone who spends all day slumped watching television.

clue.text: (& 12ac.) Sort of sex with old lover in the morning is a test

parts.note: a kind of sex performed with the mouth
an ex is a former partner
a.m. marks the morning hours

explanation.surface: A morning romp with a former partner as a trial of the relationship.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans two grid entries: the first word here, the second at 12 across.
explanation.definitionFit: An oral exam is an assessment answered by speaking rather than writing, so it is one form of examination.

clue.text: Slap balls with end of paddle? Mistake!

indicators.note: to balls something up is to make a mess of it, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: last letter

explanation.surface: A spanking scene with a paddle that goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' is British slang for making a mess, as in 'balls it up', so it signals rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapse is a slip or brief failure of attention, a small error of judgement or memory.

clue.text: Stupid sort of deputy initially subordinate to principal

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: first letter
below in rank
a school principal is the head

explanation.surface: A dim deputy head who answers to the school principal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stupid sort of deputy' reads as one phrase, but it breaks after 'sort'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dunderhead is a slow-witted person, informal for someone foolish.

clue.text: Impatient Conservative right wing's unbridled rage

indicators.note: the right wing of a written word is its final edge, so only the last letter is taken

parts.note: last letter

indicators.note: unbridled means uncontrolled and running wild, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The fury of the Tory right, impatient to have its way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right wing' looks political but means the right-hand end of the word, its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Being eager means keenly wanting something to happen soon, which is close to being impatient.

clue.text: Calculating type of county politician — true dud

parts.note: Co. is the abbreviation for county

indicators.note: a dud is faulty and broken, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: Member of Parliament
taken as written

explanation.surface: A scheming local politician who turns out to be useless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calculating' reads as scheming; the answer is a machine that literally calculates.
explanation.definitionFit: A computer is a machine built to perform calculations, so it is literally a thing that calculates.

clue.text: Supporter: "It's good when ex-president loses his head"

indicators.note: losing the head means losing the top, so the first letter is removed

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
Jimmy Carter, former US president

explanation.surface: A fan cheering the beheading of a former head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' suggests a fan, but it is a band that holds up a stocking.
explanation.definitionFit: A garter is an elastic band worn to hold up a stocking or sock, so it supports clothing.

clue.text: Learn to relax after useless leader's summing up of the recent state of British politics?

definitions.text: summing up of the recent state of British politics?

indicators.note: a leader goes first, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: first letter

indicators.note: to relax is to loosen, so these letters shake loose into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to calm down under an incompetent prime minister, and a verdict on British politics lately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the shuffled letters behind the single letter. The definition is a whole phrase, a jokey description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Unreal is slang for unbelievable or bizarre, a fair one-word verdict on the chaotic run of recent prime ministers.

clue.text: Charity takes Es before start of sex in grand surroundings

indicators.note: surroundings go all round, so one piece encloses the others

parts.note: large means big or grand
taken as written; E is also slang for an ecstasy tablet

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: A charity bash where guests take ecstasy before sex in a lavish setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' puts ES ahead of S; the pair then goes inside the word for grand.
explanation.definitionFit: Largesse is generous giving of money or gifts, especially by the wealthy, so it is a form of charity.
